Dear Rugesh,



Australia's housing market is showing early signs of stabilisation, with Cotality's August 2025 Housing Value Index reporting a modest 0.6% national increase in dwelling values through July.



Read on for our wrap up of the latest property news.

Signs of stability as housing market levels out



Australia's housing market is showing early signs of stabilisation, with Cotality's August 2025 Housing Value Index reporting a modest 0.6% national increase in dwelling values through July. While this marks the sixth consecutive monthly rise, the pace remains measured and uneven, offering mixed signals for both homeowners and first-homebuyers.



At a national level, housing values have now risen 3.7% over the past year, reflecting improved sentiment, stronger migration trends, and a continued mismatch between supply and demand. However, affordability constraints remain front of mind for many would-be buyers, particularly in cities where prices have already surged well beyond median household incomes.



For those already in the market, the latest figures may offer a sense of renewed confidence. Homeowners in Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane saw the strongest monthly gains - 0.9% 0.7% and 0.7% respectively-while Sydney and Melbourne recorded more subdued increases of 0.6% and 0.4%. Regional markets also ticked higher, particularly in Queensland and Western Australia.

 

However, Cotality's data shows the market is far from uniform. Several areas are still seeing values fall or flatten, notably parts of regional Victoria and New South Wales. This reflects the complexity of today's market, where lending conditions, interest rate expectations and local supply constraints are all pulling in different directions.



For first-home buyers, the outlook remains challenging. Despite some easing in growth rates, property values remain historically high in most capitals. At the same time, tight rental markets and rising rents are placing pressure on households trying to save for a deposit. Core fundamentals-such as low housing supply, population growth and a relatively resilient labour market-continue to support values in many areas, making meaningful price corrections unlikely in the near term.



That said, the current environment is not without opportunity. Buyers able to act with finance pre-approval and realistic expectations may find some negotiating power in pockets of slower market activity. Cotality also notes that new listing volumes are gradually increasing, which may ease some competition and broaden choice through the spring selling season.



From a policy and planning perspective, the report reinforces the need for long-term housing supply strategies. With building approvals still below pre-COVID levels and construction costs elevated, supply challenges are expected to persist-a factor that continues to underpin national housing values.



Overall, while Australia's housing market is moving gradually upwards, conditions vary widely depending on location and property type. For those looking to enter the market, seeking expert guidance and understanding local dynamics remains essential.



The market is neither booming nor busting-and for many, that may be a welcome shift.

Downsizing your home can be a smart and rewarding step-whether you're seeking a simpler lifestyle, cutting costs, or unlocking equity. But timing and planning are everything. 

Start by considering your long-term needs. Think beyond floorplan: proximity to healthcare, public transport, and family matters just as much. Assess what you truly need from your next property. Two spare bedrooms might be more than you'll actually use.



Financial clarity is key. Understand the cost of selling, buying, moving and, if relevant, aged care. Speak to your accountant or financial adviser about the federal downsizer contribution scheme, which allows eligible homeowners to contribute up to $300,000 from the sale of their home into superannuation.



Decluttering early can ease the process. Downsizing isn't just physical-it's emotional too. Take your time letting go of items that won't fit the next chapter.



Finally, don't rush. Explore the market and work with an experienced local agent who understands the lifestyle you're after. Downsizing doesn't mean compromising-it means realigning your home with the way you want to live today. Done right, it can be a liberating and financially sensible move.

Energy-efficient homes attract buyers

Energy efficiency is no longer just a buzzword-it's increasingly a key driver of residential property value across Australia. For homeowners, investing in energy-efficient upgrades isn't just good for the environment; it can also add meaningful value when it comes time to sell.



As power prices remain high and sustainability gains traction with buyers, energy-efficient homes are commanding stronger buyer interest and, in many cases, premium sale prices. Features such as solar panels, double glazing, insulation, and energy-efficient appliances are no longer niche. They are fast becoming buyer expectations, particularly among younger and environmentally conscious purchasers.



A 2023 Domain Sustainability in Property report found that homes with energy-saving features consistently sold faster and, in some cases, for up to17% more than comparable homes without them. While premiums vary by location and market cycle, the trend is clear: buyers are actively factoring energy costs and performance into their decision-making.



For homeowners, this presents both an opportunity and a responsibility. Simple improvements-such as LED lighting, window seals, or solar hot water systems-can reduce energy bills and improve comfort while strengthening market appeal. Larger upgrades, including rooftop solar, battery storage, or reverse-cycle heating and cooling, often deliver a return through both savings and increased property value.



Mandatory disclosure laws are also evolving. In the ACT, homes are already required to display an Energy Efficiency Rating (EER) at sale. Other states are actively exploring similar schemes. As this becomes the norm, properties with low ratings may face longer time on market or lower offers.

 

Lenders are responding, too. Some banks now offer green home loans or discounted mortgage rates for energy-efficient properties. This can further increase buyer interest in sustainable homes, particularly at a time when borrowing power is under pressure.



Importantly, energy efficiency can also provide greater resilience. Homes with quality insulation and passive design features remain more comfortable during heatwaves or cold snaps-reducing reliance on heating and cooling systems. That's increasingly relevant as extreme weather events become more frequent.



From a resale perspective, making your home more energy efficient is now as important as updating kitchens or bathrooms. Buyers want to know that the home they're purchasing won't cost a fortune to run or require expensive retrofits in the years ahead.



For those considering selling in the next few years, now is the time to plan upgrades. Even modest improvements can differentiate your property in a competitive market. Be sure to retain documentation-such as energy performance certificates, appliance ratings, or solar installation details-as buyers and their agents will increasingly ask for these.



Ultimately, a more energy-efficient home benefits everyone. It lowers ongoing costs, reduces carbon emissions, and supports healthier, more comfortable living. And in today's housing market, that's a value proposition buyers are increasingly prepared to pay for.
